body:
What is a tsunami?

A tsunami is a series of long ocean waves generated by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water.

Unlike ordinary sea waves, which are generated mainly by wind, tsunamis usually originate from major disturbances affecting the water column. The most common cause of destructive ocean-wide tsunamis is a large submarine earthquake.

How an earthquake generates a tsunami

At a subduction zone, one tectonic plate descends beneath another. Parts of the plate boundary may become locked, allowing stress to accumulate. During a major earthquake, sudden movement may cause the overlying seabed to rise or fall.

The vertical displacement of the seabed displaces the water above it. Gravity causes the disturbed water surface to readjust, generating waves that propagate away from the source.

Not all submarine earthquakes generate tsunamis. The likelihood of a significant tsunami depends on the earthquake's magnitude, focal depth, fault movement and ability to displace a large volume of water.

Large, shallow undersea earthquakes involving substantial vertical seabed displacement are especially capable of generating tsunamis. Predominantly horizontal fault movements are generally less effective, although they can generate tsunamis indirectly through submarine landslides or other mechanisms.

Other causes

  • Submarine or coastal landslides.
  • Volcanic explosions and volcanic flank or caldera collapse.
  • Large meteorite impacts into water.

Behaviour in deep and shallow water

In the deep ocean, a tsunami can travel rapidly while having a relatively low wave height and very long wavelength. Ships in deep water may barely notice its passage.

As the tsunami enters shallower coastal water, its speed decreases and its wavelength becomes shorter. Under suitable coastal conditions, its height increases considerably, producing powerful inundation and currents.

This behaviour explains why a tsunami that is relatively inconspicuous in the open ocean can become destructive near the coast.

Tsunamis and ordinary sea waves

PropertyTsunamiOrdinary wind wave
Main originSudden water displacementWind acting on water
WavelengthVery longMuch shorter
Water movementInvolves the water columnMainly near the surface in deep water

A tsunami is also different from a storm surge, which is an abnormal coastal water-level rise caused principally by strong winds and atmospheric pressure changes during storms. Tsunamis are not generated by ordinary gravitational tides.

The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami

On 26 December 2004, a massive undersea earthquake near northern Sumatra generated a destructive tsunami across the Indian Ocean. In India, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and several coastal areas, particularly along the eastern coast, were severely affected.

The Indian Ocean contains two major potential earthquake-generated tsunami source regions:

  • Andaman–Nicobar–Sumatra subduction zone: An important source of tsunami hazard in the eastern Indian Ocean.
  • Makran subduction zone: Located north of the Arabian Sea, near the coasts of Iran and Pakistan. It is particularly relevant to tsunami hazard assessment along India's western coast, including Gujarat.

Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre

The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) was inaugurated on 15 October 2007 at the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.

The warning system combines seismic observations, ocean-level measurements and estimates of tsunami propagation. Seismic networks identify potentially tsunamigenic earthquakes. Deep-ocean bottom-pressure sensors and coastal tide gauges provide observations of sea-level disturbances.

This combination allows authorities to assess the threat and issue suitable tsunami advisories. It does not prevent the initiating earthquake or provide an exact prediction of when that earthquake will occur.

Natural warning signs and safety

Strong or prolonged coastal earthquake shaking, unusual withdrawal or rise of seawater, and a loud ocean roar can indicate an approaching tsunami. People in vulnerable coastal areas should move to higher ground or inland without waiting for an official warning when natural warning signs indicate danger.

A tsunami consists of multiple waves. The first wave is not necessarily the largest, and dangerous currents may continue for a prolonged period. Return to affected coastal areas only after authorities declare them safe.

Prelims focus

  • Vertical seabed displacement is a major mechanism of tsunami generation.
  • Tsunami speed decreases as water becomes shallower.
  • The Indian Ocean tsunami occurred on 26 December 2004.
  • The Makran subduction zone is relevant to Gujarat's tsunami hazard.
  • ITEWC operates at INCOIS, Hyderabad, and was inaugurated in 2007.
  • Trap: Every submarine earthquake does not produce a tsunami.

[References: NOAA, The Science Behind Tsunamis, Tsunami Generation: Earthquakes and Tsunami Propagation; Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Tsunamigenic Source Identification and Indian Tsunami Early Warning System; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Press Information Bureau, 12 February 2026, tsunami early warning information. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of volcanism

Volcanism is the set of processes through which magma moves within the Earth and, in some cases, reaches its surface together with gases and fragmented rock material. It is an important endogenic process responsible for the formation of new rocks, volcanic mountains, islands and plateaus.

A volcano is an opening or vent through which molten rock, gases and fragmented materials can escape from the Earth's interior. The landform built around the opening is also commonly called a volcano.

Magma and lava

Magma is molten or partially molten rock material beneath the Earth's surface. It may contain dissolved gases, suspended mineral crystals and liquid rock.

When magma erupts onto the Earth's surface, its molten rock component is called lava. Lava cools and solidifies to form extrusive igneous rocks, such as basalt.

Magma that cools and solidifies beneath the Earth's surface forms intrusive igneous rocks, such as granite. Underground magma generally cools more slowly, allowing larger mineral crystals to develop.

How magma forms

The Earth's mantle is predominantly solid. Magma forms when particular regions of the mantle or crust undergo partial melting under suitable conditions.

Decompression melting

When hot mantle material rises, the pressure acting upon it decreases. Under suitable conditions, this reduction in pressure allows partial melting without requiring a corresponding rise in temperature. This process is particularly important beneath mid-ocean ridges and many volcanic hotspots.

Melting aided by water and other volatile substances

At subduction zones, a descending oceanic plate releases water and other volatile substances into the overlying mantle. These substances lower the temperature required for melting and promote magma formation.

Heat transfer

Hot magma entering cooler crustal rocks can transfer heat to its surroundings and cause partial melting under suitable conditions.

Structure of a volcano

  • Magma chamber: An underground region in which magma accumulates or is stored.
  • Conduit: A passage through which magma and gases move towards the surface.
  • Vent: An opening through which volcanic material is discharged.
  • Crater: A depression surrounding or associated with a volcanic vent.
  • Volcanic cone: An elevated landform built by accumulated lava or fragmented volcanic deposits.
  • Secondary vent: An additional opening through which volcanic material may erupt.

Why magma rises and erupts

Magma can rise because it is often less dense than the surrounding solid rock. Existing fractures and newly formed openings provide routes through which it can move.

As magma approaches the surface, pressure decreases and dissolved gases may separate from the melt and form bubbles. The expansion of these gases can contribute to the pressure driving an eruption.

Whether the eruption is gentle or explosive depends on several factors, including magma viscosity, temperature, gas content, the ease with which gases escape and interaction with external water.

The formation of magma does not guarantee a volcanic eruption. Much magma cools and solidifies underground without reaching the surface.

Prelims focus

  • Magma occurs beneath the surface; lava is erupted molten rock.
  • Basalt is a typical extrusive igneous rock.
  • Granite is a typical intrusive igneous rock.
  • Decompression melting occurs at divergent boundaries.
  • Water released from subducting plates promotes melting in the overlying mantle.
  • Trap: Magma formation does not mean that the entire mantle is liquid.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 7–9, and Chapter 3, p. 13; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapter 10, pp. 53–58; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 22–25; US Geological Survey, How Do Volcanoes Erupt?; NOAA JetStream, Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Viscosity and volcanic behaviour

Volcanic eruptions differ in their violence, duration and products. An important factor controlling eruption behaviour is viscosity, which is a material's resistance to flow.

Magma containing relatively little silica is generally more fluid than magma with high silica content. Temperature, crystals and dissolved gases also influence its viscosity.

Fluid magma usually allows gas bubbles to escape more readily. Highly viscous magma tends to trap expanding gases, increasing the possibility of explosive fragmentation.

Effusive and explosive eruptions

PropertyEffusive eruptionExplosive eruption
Typical magmaRelatively fluidRelatively viscous and gas-bearing
Gas escapeGenerally easierOften restricted
Dominant activityLava outpouringRapid fragmentation and ejection
Common productsLava flowsAsh, fragmented rocks and gases

Effusive eruptions

Effusive eruptions are dominated by the outpouring of lava. Fluid basaltic lava may travel considerable distances before solidifying. Repeated flows can create extensive lava plateaus or broad shield volcanoes.

Explosive eruptions

Explosive eruptions involve rapid gas expansion and fragmentation of magma and surrounding rocks. They may produce tall eruption columns, widespread ashfall and dangerous pyroclastic density currents.

Although silica-rich magma is commonly associated with explosive activity, basaltic eruptions can also become explosive when gas-rich magma fragments or when hot magma interacts with external water.

Effusive and explosive behaviour are not mutually exclusive characteristics of individual volcanoes. A single volcano may exhibit both types of activity during different stages of an eruption or throughout its history.

Central and fissure eruptions

Volcanic eruptions may also be classified according to the shape and arrangement of the surface openings.

  • Central eruption: Material emerges mainly through a central vent. Repeated accumulation around the vent may produce a volcanic cone.
  • Fissure eruption: Lava or other material emerges through elongated cracks in the Earth's surface. Extensive basaltic fissure eruptions can cover large areas with successive lava flows.

The terms central and fissure describe the arrangement of openings, whereas the terms effusive and explosive describe eruption behaviour.

Classification according to activity

  • Active volcano: A volcano that is erupting, has erupted in the recent geological past or otherwise retains the potential for renewed activity.
  • Dormant volcano: A volcano that is presently quiet but may erupt again.
  • Extinct volcano: A volcano considered unlikely to erupt again because its magmatic system is no longer expected to remain active.

These are conventional categories rather than universally fixed time-based classifications. A volcano that has not erupted within recorded human history is not automatically extinct.

Materials released during volcanic eruptions

Liquid material

Lava is the molten rock discharged at the surface. Basaltic lava is relatively rich in iron and magnesium and contains less silica than rhyolitic lava. Rhyolitic lava is silica-rich and generally more viscous. Andesitic lava has an intermediate composition.

Solid material

Fragmented material ejected during volcanic activity is collectively called tephra. Important forms include fine volcanic ash, small rock fragments called lapilli, volcanic bombs and blocks.

Volcanic ash consists of very small fragments of rock, minerals and volcanic glass. It is not equivalent to the ash produced by burning wood or other organic material.

Volcanic bombs are ejected while molten or partially molten, whereas volcanic blocks are fragments that are solid when ejected.

Gaseous material

Water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide are important volcanic gases. Hydrogen sulphide and other sulphur compounds, nitrogen compounds and smaller quantities of other gases may also be present.

Volcanic eruptions may release solids, liquids and gases simultaneously. The quantities and proportions differ between volcanoes and eruption events.

Prelims focus

  • Basaltic lava is generally more fluid than rhyolitic lava.
  • High viscosity and trapped gases favour explosive activity.
  • Fissure eruptions occur along elongated cracks.
  • Tephra refers to fragmented volcanic material.
  • Water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide are important volcanic gases.
  • Trap: Basaltic eruptions are not necessarily always non-explosive.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 23–24; US Geological Survey, How Do Volcanoes Erupt? and Volcanoes of the United States; British Geological Survey, Types of Volcano. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
